--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining; quick roll call. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE. Daniel our SE will dig into the tuning bits.
[00:08] Daniel: Hi all, Daniel here. Aisha, Liam, Priya, can you hear us okay?
[00:12] Aisha: Yep, all good. Thanks, Maya. Appreciate you taking the time.
[00:15] Priya: Hi. Quick context — we're looking at a VPC/on-prem pilot, need to hit about 200 requests per second with 95th pct latency under 300 ms for short prompts. Mixed workload though, about 60% short (<=40 tokens) and 40% longer (200-800 tokens).
[00:32] Daniel: Great, that helps. We'll focus on throughput knobs: continuous batching, scheduler windows, max_num_seqs, and token caps. Also want to talk about KV cache behavior for long-context reuse and quantization trade-offs for your hardware.
[00:42] Liam: Our infra is mostly DGX-like instances with A100s right now, but for on-prem the memory and interconnect vary — so we care about kernel selection and memory footprint.
[00:50] Daniel: Totally, that's where quantization and batching strategy change the game.
[00:55] Maya: Before we dive, quick note — we shared a benchmark template in the deck link earlier (link: https://redwood.app/benchmarks/gt-templates). Please drop traces there.
[01:10] Aisha: Will do. Ok Daniel, walk us through continuous batching — we read the docs but want concrete knobs.
[01:18] Daniel: Sure. Continuous batching in Redwood's runtime pools small incoming requests into an always-on batch window rather than only batching on arrival — think of it as sliding-window batching. The key knobs: the batch_time_ms (how long we wait to collect), max_batch_tokens (to prevent huge sequences), and max_num_seqs which caps how many sequences in a batch.
[01:36] Daniel: For mixed short/long workloads, we usually set batch_time_ms low (6-12 ms) to keep tail latency down, and set max_num_seqs to something like 12-24 depending on model memory. That allows better GPU utilization without blowing up latency.
[01:50] Aisha: We saw a note about adaptive batching — does Redwood auto-scale batch_time based on observed latency?
[01:56] Daniel: There's an adaptive mode that adjusts the batch window when throughput is high, but for predictable SLOs we prefer explicit knobs. Adaptive can be noisy with bursty traffic.
[02:06] Liam: What about scheduler priorities? We have some high-priority traffic that needs preemptive behavior.
[02:11] Daniel: We support weighted scheduling and preemptive slots. You can configure routes with priority tiers — high-priority gets smaller batch sizes and lower batch_time_ms. Lower tiers use larger batches.
[02:20] Priya: Any pitfalls when mixing quantized and full-precision models on the same pool?
[02:25] Daniel: The runtime will pick kernels based on model dtype. Mixing can cause kernel churn and lower efficiency. Best practice: separate pools per quantization profile (e.g., one pool for int8/4-bit, one for fp16).
[02:36] Aisha: We plan to try 4-bit quantization for Llama-like models; how does that impact the KV cache and prefix caching?
[02:43] Daniel: Good question. Quantization reduces memory for model weights but KV cache still uses unquantized storage in many cases — so you see memory savings primarily on model weights, less so on the cache unless you enable cache quantization (we support optional 8-bit cache compression for on-prem). That reduces memory but adds a small CPU/GPU decode cost.
[02:58] Liam: So for very long contexts the KV cache might still dominate memory?
[03:02] Daniel: Yes. If you have long repeated contexts, prefer prefix caching at the application level: store encoded KV blocks and reuse them so we avoid regenerating the same attention state. 
[03:10] Aisha: How does max_num_seqs interact with token limits? If we set max_num_seqs high, could we hit token limits and drop requests?
[03:18] Daniel: We cap both total tokens per batch (max_batch_tokens) and per-sequence token_length. The scheduler checks both: if a new request would cause the batch tokens to exceed max_batch_tokens we flush the batch. So max_num_seqs and token caps work together to avoid OOM.
[03:30] Maya: Example: for 8k context models with avg 300 tokens, setting max_num_seqs=16 would produce ~4800 tokens — within safe limits on A100. But if you have occasional 2k token requests you'd need to lower max_num_seqs or increase max_batch_tokens but also watch memory.
[03:46] Priya: Any heuristics to choose the initial max_num_seqs?
[03:50] Daniel: Start by profiling token length distribution. If 95th token length is 400, aim for max_num_seqs so that 95th * max_num_seqs <= model_token_mem_budget (we'll provide the mem budget per GPU and model). For short-prompt heavy workloads, you can be more aggressive — maybe 24 or 32.
[04:06] Aisha: We can share the token distribution.
[04:08] Daniel: Great. Also consider dynamic batching by sequence length — we can bucket by length so short prompts batch together and long ones don't drag the batch. That's a scheduler knob — "length_bucketing": true.
[04:20] Liam: About tail latency: what's typical 95th when we enable continuous batching with batch_time_ms 10 and max_num_seqs=16?
[04:27] Daniel: For a 7B model on A100 we often see 95th for short prompts around 120-180 ms with throughput ~200-300 rps. But caveat: those numbers assume KV cache hits and efficient kernels; if many long-context requests come in, tail spikes. 
[04:44] Aisha: Are there safety nets if a large request stalls the batch?
[04:48] Daniel: Yes — we have a per-request preemptive flush. If a request's expected token count exceeds a threshold it gets scheduled alone or routed to a long-tail pool. We also have time-based flush that ensures latency SLOs aren't violated.
[04:58] Priya: For on-prem VPC, how do we handle tracing and observability? We need token-level cost and latency breakdowns for audits.
[05:05] Maya: Redwood Console for private deployments supports agent-based telemetry to your monitoring stack; we can push per-request traces and KV cache hit rates into your Prometheus/Grafana. Audit logs and KMS integration are also available.
[05:16] Liam: Good. For the pilot, we'd prefer not to mix pools, but yeah separate pools for quantization sounds right.
[05:22] Daniel: Another parameter: scheduler_max_fill — controls how aggressively the scheduler tries to fill the batch before firing. Lower values mean less aggressive filling, lower latency, but lower utilization.
[05:33] Aisha: Could you give recommended starting values for our target? 200 rps mixed workload, A100s.
[05:39] Daniel: Sure: batch_time_ms = 8-12 ms, max_num_seqs = 12-16 for 7B-13B; max_batch_tokens = 12000; scheduler_max_fill = 0.75; enable length_bucketing = true; enable prefix caching for repeated prompts; separate pools for quantized models; route high-priority traffic with batch_time_ms = 4 and max_num_seqs = 6.
[05:59] Priya: We'll try those. Do you have a sample JSON config?
[06:03] Daniel: We'll share a starter config in the benchmark spreadsheet.
[06:06] Aisha: On quantization: any accuracy trade-offs you observed with 4-bit?
[06:11] Daniel: 4-bit (GPTQ-style) often has small effects on generation for some models, depending on task sensitivity. For classification/reranking it's usually fine; for creative generation you might see regressions. We recommend running evaluations on your eval packets. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles per workload.
[06:26] Liam: On memory, you mentioned cache compression. How much does 8-bit cache compression buy us?
[06:31] Daniel: Typically about 25-40% memory reduction on the KV cache depending on seq length and model. CPU/GPU decode overhead is small but measurable. We can test it in the pilot.
[06:40] Aisha: One more — how do we handle pre-warming for traffic spikes?
[06:44] Daniel: Use warm-up pools and pre-fill KV caches for known prefixes. We also support burst capacity policies to spin up extra dedicated nodes for short periods. For on-prem, that requires capacity planning but we can automate a bit.
[06:55] Priya: Ok, sounds solid. Let's talk about the perf test Daniel will run.
[07:00] Daniel: Plan: run your representative model with continuous batching enabled, set max_num_seqs=16 and then 12, measure 50/95/99 latencies and throughput. We'll run with and without cache hits (cold vs warm). We'll also try quantized version if you provide model artifacts and permission.
[07:16] Aisha: We'll share model weights and traces to the secure S3 bucket.
[07:20] Maya: I'll send the secure upload link and the benchmark spreadsheet after the call.
[07:24] Liam: Any security concerns with providing weights? We need instructions for encrypted transfer.
[07:28] Maya: We support S3 with KMS and temporary credentials; we'll include steps and a contact for our security team if you want a direct transfer.
[07:35] Priya: Good.
[07:37] Daniel: A couple of other notes: token limits at request time are enforced per-route; you can set hard caps to reject too-large requests if you prefer. Also, we surface batch composition logs so you can see which requests ended up batched together — useful to debug mixed workloads.
[07:52] Aisha: That batch composition log sounds super helpful.
[07:55] Maya: We'll enable it for the pilot.
[07:58] Priya: Any examples of failure modes you see in early pilots?
[08:02] Daniel: Biggest is mismatched pools (mixing quantized/non-quantized), underestimating KV cache memory, and relying solely on adaptive batching for a SLO-sensitive route. Those are fixable by separating pools, enabling cache compression, and pinning explicit batch_time and max_num_seqs.
[08:18] Aisha: Great. Are there any quick wins we can do in our app while Redwood tunes the runtime?
[08:23] Daniel: Yes — truncate or summarize long user inputs before sending, reuse prefix caching for repeated context, and tag high-priority low-latency routes so they go to a smaller-batch pool.
[08:33] Liam: On the pricing side, is there a cost delta for quantized pools?
[08:36] Maya: Quantized pools typically reduce GPU hours; pricing can reflect lower resource consumption. We'll include estimated unit economics in the spreadsheet for 4-bit vs fp16.
[08:46] Priya: Ok, let's cap for questions and recap next steps.
[08:50] Maya: Recap: Redwood sends benchmark spreadsheet + starter config and secure upload link; Daniel runs perf tests with max_num_seqs 16 and 12, continuous batching enabled, and reports latencies; GreenTech provides traces and model artifacts; schedule pilot kickoff week of 3/8.
[09:07] Aisha: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[09:09] Priya: Thanks.
[09:10] Liam: Thanks, talk soon.

[09:15] -- End of recorded excerpt --
